newsitem.title: USA: New document lists White House perks for donors.
newsitem.headline: New document lists White House perks for donors.

text.p: Trips with President Bill Clinton and Vice President Al Gore on Air Force One and Air Force Two were among perks proposed for major Democratic Party donors in 1994, according to a campaign document that leaked out on Friday.

The April 1994 memo, written by an unknown author, was among thousands of papers provided by former deputy chief of staff Harold Ickes to the House of Representatives Government Reform and Oversight Committee investigating Democratic Party fund-raising.
White House officials reviewed the material on Friday and spokesman Mike McCurry said they were discussing whether to make the documents public.
But the most embarrassing memo circulated widely in Washington and was openly discussed by Democratic Party co-chairs, Colorado Gov. Roy Romer and Steve Grossman.
The memo consists of a list of suggested perks that could be offered to induce big contributions to Democratic coffers as part of a drive to raise $40 million.

It was faxed to Martha Phipps, then an official with the Democratic National Committee. Grossman said whoever wrote it clearly did not know the laws governing campaign contributions, which forbid use of the White House or other official presidential premises for fund-raising.
The perks proposed by the unknown author included:
-- two seats on Air Force One and Two, the official aircraft of the President and Vice President, to be reserved for donors.
-- six seats at private White House dinners
-- six to eight spots at White House events such as jazz concerts and official visits
-- spots on official delegations abroad
-- better coordination on appointments to boards and commissions
-- the right to eat in the White house mess
-- visits to the White House and overnight stays
-- tickets at the Kennedy Centre and presidential radio addresses.
McCurry said some of the material detailed internal party matters that ought to be kept confidential.
"We will look and see exactly what he (Ickes) has produced and see if we're in a position to disclose it. I don't know the answer at this point," McCurry said.

The White House this week released several hundred pages of documents supplied to the committe by Ickes. One showed Clinton approving a proposal to invite top party donors to spend the night at the White House.
Ickes had hoped to be appointed White House Chief of Staff but the job went to Erskine Bowles, and he left the administration. He has denied he was angry at Clinton for being overlooked.
In a separate development, Clinton's Democratic Party announced it was returning $1.5 million in 1996 campaign donations that were either illegal, inappropriate or questionable.

The announcement raised to nearly $3 million the amount the Democrats have returned to donors, many of them linked to Asian business sources, since Clinton was re-elected last November as part of a growing campaign financing controversy.

Four investigations into financing activities are under way, including whether the governments of China or other countries attempted to influence U.S. policy. A federal grand jury probing the issue under the direction of a Justice Department task force heard testimony Friday from a woman who refused to identify herself to reporters afterwards.
Committees from the House of Representatives, the Senate and the Federal Election Commission are investigating reports of wrongdoing in the 1996 election campaign.
